title: Function Pointers
description: Declaring and using pointers to functions, and their classic use case: callbacks.
objectives: Declare a function pointer with a matching signature
Call a function indirectly through a function pointer
Use function pointers to implement callbacks

content.heading: Declaring and Using Function Pointers
content.body: A function pointer holds the address of a function, letting a function itself be passed around, stored in a variable, or chosen dynamically at runtime, much like data. Its declaration must match the target function's exact signature: int (*fp)(int, int); declares fp as a pointer to a function taking two ints and returning an int (the parentheses around *fp are essential — without them, int *fp(int, int); would instead declare a function returning int *, a completely different meaning). Assigning a function to a matching pointer, fp = add; (the function name decays to its address, similar to how an array name decays to a pointer, & is optional here), and calling through it, fp(2, 3); (or, equivalently, (*fp)(2, 3);), invokes the pointed-to function.

content.heading: Callbacks
content.body: The classic use case for function pointers is a callback: passing a function as an argument to another function, which then calls it back at an appropriate point — this is how the standard library's qsort() lets you supply a custom comparison function for sorting arbitrary data, and it's a general pattern for making a function's behavior configurable by the caller without needing to know in advance every possible variant of that behavior. Function pointers are also the mechanism behind implementing simple 'virtual functions'/polymorphism-like behavior manually in C, since the language has no built-in OOP inheritance/dispatch mechanism (a technique used, for instance, in the Linux kernel's driver interfaces).

content.explanation: compute() takes a function pointer as a parameter, letting the caller decide at each call site which operation actually runs — the essence of a callback.

keyPoints: A function pointer's declared type must match the target function's exact signature
int (*fp)(int, int); declares a function pointer — the parentheses around *fp are required
A function's name decays to its address; calling through a matching pointer invokes it
Callbacks (passing a function pointer as an argument) let a function's behavior be configured by its caller
commonMistakes: Omitting the parentheses around *fp in a function pointer declaration, accidentally declaring something else entirely
Assigning a function whose signature doesn't exactly match the pointer's declared type
Forgetting that calling a function through a mismatched-signature pointer is undefined behavior, even if it happens to compile with only a warning
